notes.choicesExplained: A adds a network interface in the virtual network, which the team wants to avoid. C filters traffic but doesn’t secure the service to the subnet.
notes.explanation: A virtual network rule then secures the service resources to your virtual network.
notes.evidence: Once you enable service endpoints in your virtual network, you can add a virtual network rule to secure the Azure service resources to your virtual network.
notes.source: Azure virtual network service endpoints, “Key benefits”

notes.front: A web app runs in three regions. Users worldwide need the nearest healthy region, caching, path-based routing and fast failover. What should sit in front?
notes.back: C: Azure Front Door.
notes.choices:
A) Azure Traffic Manager
B) A regional Azure Load Balancer
C) Azure Front Door
notes.choicesExplained: A works through name resolution only, with no caching or path routing, and fails over more slowly. B is regional and has no web-layer features.
notes.explanation: It is a global load balancer for web traffic with caching, path-based routing and fast failover.
notes.evidence: Azure Front Door is an application delivery network that provides global load balancing and site acceleration for web applications. It provides Layer-7 capabilities for your application such as Secure Sockets Layer (SSL) offload, path-based routing, fast failover, and caching to improve performance and high availability.
notes.source: Load balancing options, “Azure load balancing services”

notes.front: A multiplayer game uses layer 4 traffic across a scale set of virtual machines in one region and needs ultra-low latency. What should distribute the traffic?
notes.back: A: Azure Load Balancer.
notes.choices:
A) Azure Load Balancer
B) Azure Application Gateway
C) Azure Front Door
notes.choicesExplained: B and C are web-traffic load balancers aimed at application-layer features rather than layer 4 game traffic.
notes.explanation: It is a layer 4 service built for high performance and ultra-low latency.
notes.evidence: Load Balancer is a Layer-4 service that handles inbound and outbound traffic across all User Datagram Protocol (UDP) and Transmission Control Protocol (TCP) protocols. It's designed for high performance and ultra-low latency.
notes.source: Load balancing options, “Azure load balancing services”

notes.front: In one region, requests to /images must go to one server pool and /video to another, with encryption ended at the gateway. What fits?
notes.back: B: Azure Application Gateway (v2).
notes.choices:
A) Azure Load Balancer
B) Azure Application Gateway (v2)
C) Azure Traffic Manager
notes.choicesExplained: A works at layer 4 and can’t read request paths. C is global and name-based, with no path routing.
notes.explanation: It works at the application layer and terminates encrypted connections at the gateway.
notes.evidence: Application Gateway operates at the application layer (OSI layer 7) and provides features like SSL/TLS termination, autoscaling, zone redundancy, and integration with Web Application Firewall for security.
notes.source: What is Azure Application Gateway?, “What is Azure Application Gateway?”

notes.front: A non-web service runs on endpoints in two Azure regions and one on-premises site. Clients should be sent to a healthy endpoint by name resolution. What fits?
notes.back: C: Azure Traffic Manager.
notes.choices:
A) Azure Front Door
B) Azure Application Gateway
C) Azure Traffic Manager
notes.choicesExplained: A is recommended for web traffic. B is regional, so it can’t spread clients across regions and sites on its own.
notes.explanation: It directs clients through the Domain Name System and supports endpoints outside Azure.
notes.evidence: Traffic Manager uses DNS to direct client requests to the appropriate service endpoint based on a traffic-routing method. Traffic Manager also provides health monitoring for every endpoint. The endpoint can be any Internet-facing service hosted inside or outside of Azure.
notes.source: What is Azure Traffic Manager?, “What is Azure Traffic Manager?”

notes.front: ExpressRoute versus VPN Gateway: how does each carry traffic to Azure?
notes.back: ExpressRoute uses a private connection through a connectivity provider; VPN Gateway sends encrypted traffic over the public internet.
notes.explanation: VPN Gateway encrypts the traffic it sends over the internet.
notes.evidence: Azure VPN Gateway service can be used to send encrypted traffic between an Azure virtual network and on-premises locations over the public Internet.
notes.source: What is Azure VPN Gateway?, “What is Azure VPN Gateway?”

notes.front: Private endpoint versus service endpoint: what does each do to the connection?
notes.back: A private endpoint puts a network interface with a private address in your virtual network; a service endpoint switches the traffic’s source to private addresses.
notes.explanation: A service endpoint gives the Azure service your virtual network’s identity, so a virtual network rule can lock the service to that network.
notes.evidence: A virtual network service endpoint provides the identity of your virtual network to the Azure service. Once you enable service endpoints in your virtual network, you can add a virtual network rule to secure the Azure service resources to your virtual network.
notes.source: Azure virtual network service endpoints, “Secure Azure services to virtual networks”

notes.front: Azure Front Door versus Traffic Manager: which handles the traffic itself?
notes.back: Front Door handles the web traffic at layer 7; Traffic Manager only uses the Domain Name System to point clients at endpoints.
notes.explanation: Traffic Manager only answers name lookups, so clients then connect to the endpoint directly; neither it nor Load Balancer offers layer 7 features.
notes.evidence: Traffic Manager and Load Balancer can distribute any traffic type, including HTTP(S). However, these services don't provide Layer-7 capabilities. Unlike Load Balancer, Traffic Manager doesn't handle the traffic directly. Traffic Manager uses DNS to direct clients to the appropriate endpoints.
notes.source: Load balancing options, “Service categorizations”

notes.front: Global versus regional load-balancing services: what does each distribute traffic across?
notes.back: Global: regional back ends, clouds or on-premises services. Regional: virtual machines, containers or clusters within a region’s virtual network.
notes.explanation: Global services give a single control plane that routes users to available back ends worldwide.
notes.evidence: Global:** These load balancing services distribute traffic across regional back ends, clouds, or hybrid on-premises services. They provide a single control plane that routes user traffic to available back ends globally.
notes.source: Load balancing options, “Global versus regional”

notes.front: DDoS IP Protection versus DDoS Network Protection: how do they differ?
notes.back: IP Protection is paid per protected public address and lacks rapid response support, cost protection and WAF discounts; the core engineering is the same.
notes.explanation: Both tiers share the same core engineering features.
notes.evidence: DDoS IP Protection is a pay-per-protected IP model. DDoS IP Protection contains the same core engineering features as DDoS Network Protection, but will differ in the following value-added services: DDoS rapid response support, cost protection, and discounts on WAF.
notes.source: What is Azure DDoS Protection?, “Tiers”

notes.front: Virtual network peering versus global virtual network peering: what does each connect?
notes.back: Virtual network peering connects networks in the same Azure region; global peering connects networks across regions.
notes.explanation: Local and global peering are the two types of peering Azure supports.
notes.evidence: Virtual network peering**: Connect virtual networks within the same Azure region. * **Global virtual network peering**: Connect virtual networks across Azure regions.
notes.source: Azure virtual network peering, “Azure virtual network peering”
